units.text: INT. GHOSTS - CONTINUOUS
Regina--now I see it--you are going to your ruin.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Oh, stuff! Good-bye.
units.name: REGINA

units.text: She nods and goes out through the hall.
Stands at the window and looks out.
Is she gone?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Murmuring aside to himself.
I think it was a mistake, this.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Goes up behind him and lays her hands on his shoulders.
Oswald, my dear boy--has it shaken you very much?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Turns his face towards her.
All that about father, do you mean?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes, about your unhappy father. I am so afraid it may have been too much for you.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Why should you fancy that? Of course it came upon me as a great surprise; but it can make no real difference to me.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Draws her hands away.
No difference! That your father was so infinitely unhappy!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Of course I can pity him, as I would anybody else; but--
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Nothing more! Your own father!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Impatiently.
Oh, "father,"--"father"! I never knew anything of father. I remember nothing about him, except that he once made me sick.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: This is terrible to think of! Ought not a son to love his father, whatever happens?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: When a son has nothing to thank his father for? has never known him? Do you really cling to that old superstition?--you who are so enlightened in other ways?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Can it be only a superstition--?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes; surely you can see that, mother. It's one of those notions that are current in the world, and so--
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Deeply moved.
Ghosts!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Crossing the room.
Yes; you may call them ghosts.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Wildly.
Oswald--then you don't love me, either!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: You I know, at any rate--
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes, you know me; but is that all!
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: And, of course, I know how fond you are of me, and I can't but be grateful to you. And then you can be so useful to me, now that I am ill.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes, cannot I, Oswald? Oh, I could almost bless the illness that has driven you home to me. For I see very plainly that you are not mine: I have to win you.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Impatiently.
Yes yes yes; all these are just so many phrases. You must remember that I am a sick man, mother. I can't be much taken up with other people; I have enough to do thinking about myself.
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: In a low voice.
I shall be patient and easily satisfied.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: And cheerful too, mother!
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: Yes, my dear boy, you are quite right.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Goes towards him.
Have I relieved you of all remorse and self-reproach now?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Yes, you have. But now who will relieve me of the dread?
units.name: OSWALD

units.text: The dread?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Walks across the room.
